tr.td: Babrra (also spelled Babara or Babarra), Charsadda, North-West Frontier Province, Pakistan
Supporters of the Khudai Khidmatgar (Red Shirt) movement, marching against the arrest of their leaders
Blamed by Khudai Khidmatgar sources on Chief Minister Abdul Qayyum Khan, who defended the firing in the provincial assembly
Disputed: about 15 to 25 by official accounts; 600 or more by Khudai Khidmatgar accounts
Khudai Khidmatgar, founded in 1929 by Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Bacha Khan), committed to non-violence
Muslim League ministry of Abdul Qayyum Khan, installed after the elected ministry of Dr Khan Sahib was dismissed in August 1947
The North West Frontier Province Public Safety Ordinance of mid-1948, which allowed detention without stated reason
15 killed and about 40 injured (as reported by India Today); 25 killed and 35 injured (as reported by The Khyber Post)
611 killed and 1,200 injured, as claimed by Pakhtun nationalist organisations (The Friday Times)
About 45 minutes, according to two of the accounts
FIR No. 184 of 12 August 1948, Prang police station, lodged against the marchers
No independent investigation at the time (BW Times); Pakhtun nationalist leaders still demand an independent inquiry or a truth commission

li.a: The News on Sunday: The Babara massacre, then and now
The Khyber Post: The Babrra Massacre of 1948, A Forgotten Tragedy
BW Times: The tragic events of 12 August 1948 at Babrra in Charsadda
Freedom from the Forbidden (blog): The Babarra Massacre of August 12, 1948, and a Pashto song
The Friday Times: A bloody day at Babarra (archived copy)
India Today: When Jinnah's Pakistan slaughtered Frontier Gandhi's 600 unarmed Pathans

content.p: On 12 August 1948, two days before Pakistan marked its first anniversary, police in the North-West Frontier Province opened fire on a column of Khudai Khidmatgar supporters walking to a protest at Babrra, a village in Charsadda district about 40 kilometres from Peshawar. The marchers belonged to a movement built on non-violence, and they were protesting the arrest of its leaders. How many died has never been settled. Most official figures reported run from 15 to 25 dead, against Khudai Khidmatgar claims of more than 600.

No comprehensive independent investigation was carried out at the time, according to BW Times. Pakhtun nationalist politicians still ask for one, and Babrra remains a reference point in arguments over how Pakistan treated its Pashtun population in its first years. Almost every figure and motive in the story comes from one side or the other, so the accounts below are credited to those who gave them.

When the British Raj ended in 1947, the Khudai Khidmatgars, also called the Red Shirts or the Frontier Congress, were the ruling party of the North-West Frontier Province. The Friday Times reports that Dr Khan Sahib, brother of the movement's founder Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, was chief minister, and that his side held a 34 to 16 majority in the provincial assembly. On 22 August 1947, a week after Pakistan came into being, the governor dismissed that ministry and the Muslim League's Abdul Qayyum Khan was installed in its place.

The Muslim League's position, as the same article puts it, was that the Khudai Khidmatgar ministry had not attended the flag-hoisting on 15 August and that its loyalty to the new state was therefore in doubt. Others dispute that. The Friday Times quotes a letter attributed to Governor Lockhart, citing a National Archives reference, saying the League wanted the ministry dissolved before 15 August, and a message from Mountbatten to Liaquat Ali Khan that dismissing it would be undemocratic and unconstitutional. Critics read the episode as the start of horse-trading in Pakistani politics. The article also notes that Qayyum Khan had himself been a Khudai Khidmatgar until at least 1945.

The Red Shirts tried to calm matters. At a meeting at Sardaryab near Peshawar on 3 and 4 September 1947, they resolved to treat Pakistan as their own country, called the dismissal of Dr Khan Sahib's ministry undemocratic, and pledged to take no step that would make things harder for either the provincial or central government. They also cut their ties with the All India Congress and replaced the tricolour with a red flag. No reconciliation followed. According to the Friday Times, authorities alleged that Bacha Khan was planning with the Faqir of Ipi, a militant leader, to topple the government, while his supporters said Qayyum Khan had led Muhammad Ali Jinnah to believe the Red Shirts meant him harm.

In mid-1948 the provincial government issued the North West Frontier Province Public Safety Ordinance. The News on Sunday says it was promulgated in June 1948 by the governor, and describes it as letting the government detain anyone indefinitely and seize property without telling the detainee why. The blog Freedom from the Forbidden dates it to July 1948 and says detainees could not challenge their arrest in court. On 11 July 1948, The Pakistan Times, quoted by the Friday Times, wrote that the administration already had wide enough powers and advised the Qayyum ministry "to govern the province by law, and if cannot, to make room for those who can".

The News on Sunday adds that the governor stated the ordinance was issued on special orders from Governor-General Jinnah. Bacha Khan himself had been arrested: the Friday Times says he was held in Bahadur Khel village in Kohat for three years under section 40 of the Frontier Crimes Regulation. The allegation against him concerned financial support for the Faqir of Ipi. A provincial jirga of the Khudai Khidmatgars demanded that the government publish the amount and a receipt, and said that if a court proved the charge they would separate from him.

That jirga also agreed on a protest at Babrra on 12 August. The Friday Times says the government cordoned off the area a day earlier, imposed an unannounced curfew in the district and arrested thousands of Red Shirts. It cites Dr Sohail Khan of Wali Khan University, Mardan, as saying that with thousands of Khudai Khidmatgars and most of the top leadership in prison, the decision to go ahead was taken by Salar Ameen Jan, who led the procession. The Khyber Post, by contrast, names a man called Speen Malang as the leader of the gathering.

On the morning of 12 August, according to The News on Sunday, scores of Khudai Khidmatgars began assembling at Utmanzai, Bacha Khan's home town, and set out for Babrra despite the imposition of section 144, the colonial-era ban on assembly. BW Times says the authorities regarded the gathering as illegal because the organisation had been banned, that police were deployed around the area and ordered the crowd to disperse, and that witnesses recalled the protesters refusing to leave.

The Friday Times describes hundreds of Bacha Khan's followers walking toward the venue and says state forces fired on them from vantage points on surrounding buildings. The Khyber Post says the shooting began as the rally reached the Babrra ground, that many people fell where they stood, and that others drowned in the Kabul River as they tried to flee because other exits had been closed. Dr Sohail Khan, in the Friday Times, puts the number of bodies that went into the river at more than 265; the blog says 250. Both the Khyber Post and the blog say the firing lasted about 45 minutes.

The same accounts say women were in the march. Dr Sohail Khan names Taju Bibi, Wali Khan's wife, among them. The Friday Times quotes the memoir of Jehanzeb Niaz, who wrote that many women were among the injured and killed and that the rest tore their shawls to bandage the wounded. The Khyber Post repeats a story, which it presents as something that was told rather than something it verified, that village women came forward with copies of the Quran on their heads and begged for mercy while the shooting continued. In the Friday Times, Dr Sohail Khan says the first to die was Speen Malang, who was carrying the party flag.

The wounded were not safe afterwards. The News on Sunday and the Khyber Post both say hospitals were told not to admit them. The Friday Times quotes Hayat Roghani, editor of the magazine Pukhtoon, saying the order not to treat the injured came from local authorities and that dozens died of their wounds. The blog adds that doctors who tried to help were arrested and their property confiscated, a claim the other pages do not make.

The numbers divide along political lines. India Today says the government claimed 15 Khudai Khidmatgars were killed and about 40 wounded. The Khyber Post gives an official announcement of 25 killed and 35 injured. BW Times says official reports of the time spoke of 15 to 20 dead. The blog says the official count was under 200, a figure no other page here supports.

On the other side, the Khyber Post cites Khudai Khidmatgar claims of more than 600 dead and 1,200 seriously injured. In the Friday Times, Pakhtun nationalist organisations claim 611 dead and 1,200 injured. India Today, which accepts the figure of 611 in its own narration, also reports that Pyarelal, Mahatma Gandhi's secretary, wrote in his 1966 book that an eyewitness swore on the Quran that the dead numbered 2,000. BW Times concludes that because no comprehensive independent investigation was carried out at the time, the true scale has never been established.

The blog argues that families hid their dead and wounded to avoid payments demanded by the government, which would make an accurate count harder still. Whether or not that explains the gap, no source opened here offers a body-by-body list of the dead.

The chief minister did not deny the shooting. Quoted by The News on Sunday, he told the provincial assembly in September 1948: "I had imposed section 144 at Babara. When the people did not disperse, firing was opened on them. They were lucky that the police had finished ammunition; otherwise not a single soul would have been left alive and if they were killed, the government would not have cared about them." The Khyber Post gives a longer version of his speech that includes the words "Khudai khidmatgar members are traitors to the country".

The Friday Times reports that his administration maintained that section 144 had been announced and the protesters were therefore challenging the government's authority. The late politician Wali Khan, in his book on Bacha Khan, disputed this, saying the Deputy Commissioner of Charsadda, Hidayat Ullah Khan Toru, had told him that he had neither been asked to impose section 144 nor had imposed it. That is a recollection relayed by Wali Khan, and the pages do not show the original order either way.

After the firing, police lodged FIR No. 184, dated 12 August 1948, at Prang police station, against the marchers, the Friday Times says. The paper also reports that the government blew up the Khudai Khidmatgars' central office at Sardaryab and began a wider crackdown, which many took to be an attempt to eliminate the Red Shirts as a political force.

A grievance that has lasted as long as the shooting itself is the money. The Friday Times quotes Afrasiab Khattak of the Awami National Party, heir to Bacha Khan's political legacy, saying the Khudai Khidmatgars were fined 50,000 rupees in 1948, which he describes as the cost of the operation. The blog repeats the figure and says properties were also confiscated. The Friday Times records the account of Murad Ali, whose father Sultan Kaka of Prang was in the rally and who told his son he had buried six bodies in one grave because the authorities were collecting 50 rupees in fines per grave and 100 rupees per injured person. Both are accounts from the movement's side; no government document on the fines is cited in the pages opened.
content.h2: Memory and the call for an inquiry
content.p: The News on Sunday notes that the country celebrated its first independence anniversary two days later, and that the massacre was passed down largely as folklore. The Friday Times says the memory is strongest among Pakhtun nationalist organisations and largely absent outside Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Huseyn Shaheed Suhrawardy, speaking in Dhaka in July 1950, called the killing worse than Jallianwala Bagh, according to both The News on Sunday and India Today. Bacha Khan told the assembly on 20 March 1954 that a tribunal should look into loyalty or treason and also into "the general massacre, arson and loot" at Charsadda, as The News on Sunday quotes him. India Today says the Awami National Party calls Babrra the "Karbala of Pashtuns".

Khattak told the Friday Times that his party wants a Truth and Reconciliation Commission to examine such cases and assign responsibility, after which Babrra could be closed. Hayat Roghani told the paper that when Bacha Khan was freed and returned to Sardaryab, he answered talk of revenge by saying the movement's path was non-violence. The Friday Times quotes him: "Our path was non-violence and it will be the same!" Khattak argues that the events of 1948 left the country's ruling elite doubting the loyalty of Pashtun nationalists, a suspicion he says never went away.
